cases.question: Which games dominated the interview, and was there a single third-place game?
cases.query: most discussed games Stadium Events Battleship Mega Man Urban Strike Chubby Cherub Castlevania Legends Super Metroid Fusion Zero Mission
cases.answer: Stadium Events leads with three meaningful paragraphs in this untimed map. Eight games tie at two: Battleship, Mega Man for Game Gear, Urban Strike, Chubby Cherub, Castlevania Legends, Super Metroid, Metroid Fusion and Zero Mission. There is no unique second- or third-place game. Much of this is acquisition, missing-component or collecting discussion rather than gameplay. Battleship's imagined future completion joke in Paragraph 43 does not earn another meaningful paragraph. Collection sets, sites, hardware, broad series and the ambiguous raw Sixth fragment are excluded; paragraph coverage is not minutes or a favorites ranking.
cases.reason: P35–54 source and independent union confirm Stadium3 and eight games2; Battleship P43 joke excluded and no unique third.

cases.question: Who was interviewed, and is Kat's John the same person as the cohost?
cases.query: Dain Dane Anderson guest Kat Johnny John husband roster
cases.answer: The hosts are Kat and Johnny, interviewing Nintendo Age founder Dain Anderson, whose name appears as Dane and other variants in the captions. Kat's John is explicitly explained as her husband, not Johnny. Her shared collecting story belongs to that marriage, not a partnership with the cohost. Tyler is not a participant in this source.
cases.reason: Opening roster establishes Dain as guest with Kat/Johnny; partner John is not cohost or Tyler.

cases.question: Why did the site take years to open after it was built?
cases.query: Nintendo Age 2001 five years confidence National Game Depot release
cases.answer: Dain says he and National Game Depot built the site around 2001 but he sat on it for about five years. He links the delay to low confidence and reluctance to invite Internet criticism; his collaborator eventually encouraged him to release it and improve it afterward. The approaching ten-year anniversary refers to the public site, not the beginning of development. His design rule is to build what he personally wants first, which he says helps sustain his enthusiasm. These are his retrospective explanations, not a diagnosis.
cases.reason: P2–6 distinguish2001 development,2006 public launch and confidence/delay, not a falsely exact SegaAge date.

cases.question: Had PlayStation Age already replaced the old site during this interview?
cases.query: PlayStation Collecting Age rename remaining share domain final touches
cases.answer: No completed rename is reported. Dain says he had co-owned PlayStation Collecting with its previous operator, bought the remaining share the prior year, and was making final touches for the PlayStation Age name, probably within the next few weeks. The domain and launch discussion is prospective. Sega Age's suggested 2010 start is not confidently confirmed by him either.
cases.reason: P4–5 report prior acquisition of PlayStationCollecting and intended rename, not verified completed launch.

cases.question: Why didn't the Nintendo Age database contain every collecting detail?
cases.query: database forums variants organic Nintendo Canada list cardboard
cases.answer: Dain describes a moving target: each attempt to model variants uncovered another layer, so he leaned toward organic contributions. Johnny similarly limited his cardboard project to major variants instead of every packing detail. A requested all-region NES list from a Nintendo of Canada contact never arrived; that does not establish that no internal list existed. Dain says the forums contain more information than the database, so the two sources complement one another rather than either being exhaustive.
forbidden: official company has no records proved
cases.reason: P7–10 and29–30 distinguish catalog limits, variants and deeper forum knowledge; undelivered Nintendo list proves no absence.

cases.question: Did Dain see Instagram or Atari Age as enemies of Nintendo Age?
cases.query: Instagram Atari Age Digital Press hobby twenty friends
cases.answer: He describes competition for attention but not a war: he calls the site a hobby and says even 20 friends would make it worthwhile. Instagram's simple visual sharing and the forums' deeper accumulated knowledge serve different needs, and people can use both. Atari Age was an inspiration, not the same ownership umbrella, and Dain describes friendly relationships with other community operators. His comments describe the 2016 conversation, not current platform conditions.
cases.reason: P11–30 describe contacts, trades, feedback and social/forum complements, not perfect trust or platform war.

cases.question: Did Dain abandon NES collecting after completing other systems?
cases.query: Dain refocus NES Game Boy complete N64 Super Nintendo 85 Atari
cases.answer: He moved in the opposite direction: during the preceding two years he had been refocusing on NES because it made him happier. He reports having completed Game Boy, Game Boy Color and N64 sets, about 85% of Super Nintendo, just about every Sega set and an Atari 2600 collection fewer than 20 games short. Those are qualified historical scopes, not proof he still retained everything. NES is his beloved platform, while Game Boy was his most enjoyable collection to build; those statements address different kinds of enjoyment.
cases.reason: P30–38 distinguish historical wide sets from later NES focus and enjoyment of GameBoy collecting.

cases.question: What made the supposedly common handheld sets difficult to finish?
cases.query: boxed Game Boy Color Rhino Rumble ISS 99 Nicktoons Racing Game Gear
cases.answer: The recurring distinction is carts versus boxes: plentiful cartridges do not make a boxed set easy. Dain names Rhino Rumble and ISS 99 among tough Game Boy Color boxes and says finding a Nicktoons Racing box took about five months. He mentions roughly ten difficult games but does not supply a complete ten-title list. Game Gear brings similar problems, including Urban Strike's box; Dain sold his set before obtaining that box. His under $10,000 Game Boy recollection is a historical total, not a current budget promise.
cases.reason: P34–37 supply three named difficult GBC boxes, unfinished GG Urban Strike box and uncertain raw Sixth, not a complete ten-title list.

cases.question: How did Dain finally get Stadium Events without paying cash for it?
cases.query: Dain Stadium Events traded Atari 2600 money favorite white whale
cases.answer: Dain says he traded his Atari 2600 collection for Stadium Events and the other party added money to the deal. He felt it cost him dearly in collecting terms and was not a good deal for him, but it let him obtain the game without spending cash. This completed his NES set as he defines it. Stadium Events is his physical favorite piece; his metaphorical favorite is whatever game is coming in the mail, not a named gameplay favorite.
cases.reason: P41–42 explicitly put Atari collection outgoing and money incoming with Stadium Events, not cash-only purchase.
